lessons.title: 3 Python Automation Projects for Beginners
objectives: Recognise the shape of a task that is worth automating
Read someone else's automation and see the pattern underneath it
Judge which of your own repeated chores are real candidates
lessons.notes:
WATCH THIS VIDEO TWICE, IN TWO DIFFERENT LESSONS. Here, in module 6, watch it straight through WITHOUT TYPING ANYTHING. You are reading for the pattern. In module 7 you come back to the same video and build one of the projects line by line. Trying to do both at once is why people finish a tutorial with working code and no idea how to write their own.

THE THREE TESTS. A task is worth automating when all three are true. One, it is REPEATED - you will do it again next week. Two, it is RULE-BASED - you could write down exactly what you do, with no judgement calls. Three, the input ALREADY EXISTS AS DATA - in a file, a spreadsheet, a page - rather than in your head or on paper.

ALL THREE PROJECTS ARE THE SAME SHAPE: read something, decide something, write something out. Renaming files reads filenames, applies a rule, writes new names. The spreadsheet project reads rows, filters them, sends messages. Once you see that shape you will see it everywhere, and every automation you ever write is a version of it.

WHAT IS NOT WORTH AUTOMATING. A thing done once. A thing whose rule changes every time you do it. A thing where the input arrives as a photo of a handwritten book - the reading step costs more than the whole chore does by hand.

DO THE TIME MATHS BEFORE YOU START, not after. A script that takes four hours to write and saves ten minutes a week pays for itself in twenty-four weeks. That is clearly worth it for something you will keep doing for a year, and clearly not worth it for a one-off. Beginners skip this sum and then feel cheated.

CANDIDATES AROUND YOU. A shop owner who copies M-Pesa statement lines into a spreadsheet every evening. A school secretary renaming and filing hundreds of scanned forms. Someone who downloads the same report from a portal each Monday and reformats it by hand. These are ordinary chores in ordinary Kenyan offices and they pass all three tests.

READ THE CODE, DO NOT COPY IT YET. Pause at the end of each project and say in one sentence what it reads, what it decides, and what it writes. If you cannot say those three things, rewind. That sentence is the thing you are here for - the code you can always look up again.
lessons.practice: List five things you, or someone you know, does repeatedly on a computer. Score each one against the three tests: repeated, rule-based, input already exists as data. Pick the one that scores highest and write three sentences about it - what it reads, what it decides, what it writes. Keep that note. Module 7 builds it.

quiz.question: What are the three tests that a task is worth automating?
options: It is repeated, it is rule-based, and its input already exists as data
It is difficult, it is important, and it is urgent
It uses a library, it runs fast, and the code is short
It appeared in a tutorial you have watched

quiz.question: A script would take four hours to write and would save ten minutes a week. What should you do?
options: Work out the payback period first, and judge it against how long you will keep doing the task
Never automate it, because four hours is too long to spend
Always automate it, because automation is always worth it
Automate it only if the finished code is short

lessons.title: How to Land Freelance Jobs with Python
objectives: Know what beginner Python freelance work actually consists of
Judge honestly where you stand against what clients pay for
Decide the realistic first step from where you are
lessons.notes:
THIS VIDEO IS USED TWICE. In this lesson watch the OPENING SECTION, where he describes the kinds of jobs that exist and who buys them. The question here is what this work really is and whether it is realistic for you. Module 8 returns to the same video for the second half - profiles, proposals and pricing - once you have something finished to sell.

THE HONEST OPENING. Most beginner Python freelance work is not building apps. It is small, unglamorous data work: cleaning a spreadsheet somebody exported badly, pulling a list out of a directory, turning a hundred PDF files into one CSV, writing a script that renames and files images. It pays modestly. It is real work and people pay for it every day.

WHAT CLIENTS ARE ACTUALLY BUYING is not Python. It is hours back. Nobody has ever hired anyone because they used a for loop. They hire because their Tuesday evening is gone every week and they want it returned.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART. The global freelance marketplaces are crowded and priced accordingly. A new profile with no reviews is competing with thousands of others, many of them experienced and cheaper than you expect. That is not a reason to give up; it is a reason to understand that THE FIRST JOB ALMOST NEVER COMES FROM COLD BIDDING. It comes from somebody who already knows you - the shop, the school, the church, the sacco, the small business a relative runs.

A REALISTIC TIMELINE. From a standing start, expect three to six months of consistent practice before you can take money for work and deliver it without panic. Anyone promising two weeks is selling a course.

GETTING PAID FROM HERE. Work out how the money will actually reach you BEFORE you accept a job. Some platforms pay out in ways that are awkward or expensive from Kenya, and some clients will propose a method that suits them and not you. Agree the method in writing before you start. A job you cannot get paid for is not a job, it is a hobby with a deadline.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD OF BIDDING FIRST. Do one piece of work for somebody local, free or nearly free, with their permission to describe it afterwards. That gives you a result you can state as a number - an evening task cut from three hours to four minutes - and a number like that is worth more than any certificate you can buy.
lessons.practice: Write down three people or small businesses you already have access to who do repetitive computer work. For each, write one sentence describing the chore and one sentence estimating how many hours a month it costs them. Then write, honestly, what you would still need to learn to take it on. Do not contact anyone yet - module 8 covers the approach.

quiz.question: What does most beginner Python freelance work actually consist of?
options: Small data chores - cleaning spreadsheets, pulling lists, converting files, renaming and filing
Building mobile applications for startups
Training machine learning models
Maintaining large company websites

quiz.question: Where does a first paid job most often come from?
options: Somebody who already knows you locally, not a cold bid on a crowded marketplace
The lowest bid on a global freelance platform
A certificate from an online course
A social media post asking for work

lessons.title: Build a Web Scraper with Beautiful Soup
objectives: Build a scraper that reads a page and writes a clean file
Know what you may and may not scrape, and how to be a polite visitor
Survive a page that changes or a run that dies halfway
lessons.notes:
WHAT A SCRAPER IS: a program that fetches a web page and pulls named pieces out of it. Two libraries do the work - one to fetch the page, one to read the HTML you get back.

THE SHAPE IS THE SAME AS EVERY AUTOMATION: fetch the page, find the repeating container - one listing, one row, one card - loop over those containers, pull the fields you want out of each, write them to a CSV. Read, decide, write.

INSPECT BEFORE YOU CODE. Open the page in your browser, right-click the thing you want and choose Inspect. You are looking for the tag and class that wraps ONE item. Write that selector down on paper before you type a line. People who skip this step spend an hour guessing.

BE A POLITE VISITOR. Most tutorials skip this and it is the part that gets beginners into trouble. Check the site's terms and its robots file before you start. PUT A DELAY of a second or two between requests - a loop with no delay is indistinguishable from an attack and will get your address blocked, sometimes permanently. Take only the fields you actually need. DO NOT SCRAPE PERSONAL DATA - names, phone numbers, email addresses of individuals - and do not build or resell a harvested contact list. Kenya's Data Protection Act treats personal data seriously, and a client who asks you to collect phone numbers is asking you to carry the risk on their behalf. Say no, and say why.

IT WILL BREAK, AND HERE IS WHY. Sites change their markup without warning. A scraper that worked yesterday and returns nothing today has almost always hit a renamed class, not a bug in your logic. PRINT WHAT YOU ACTUALLY RECEIVED before you start debugging what you expected to receive. That one habit will save you more hours than any other in this course.

WRITE EACH ROW AS YOU GO, rather than collecting everything in memory and saving at the end. A run that dies at item four hundred of five hundred should leave you three hundred and ninety-nine good rows, not an empty file. On a connection that drops, that is the difference between a small annoyance and a lost evening.

DATA COSTS MONEY. Every page you fetch comes out of a bundle. Test your loop on three pages before you point it at three hundred, and print the count as it runs so you can stop it.
lessons.practice: Build a scraper against a site that permits it - a public listing page carrying no personal data - that reads at least ten items and writes them to a CSV with three columns. Include a delay between requests and write each row as you go. Then break it on purpose by changing the selector, and read what your program prints when it finds nothing.

quiz.question: Why should you put a delay between requests?
options: A loop with no delay looks like an attack and gets your address blocked - a polite scraper waits
It makes the code easier for other people to read
Python cannot fetch two pages in quick succession
It makes the resulting CSV file smaller

quiz.question: Your scraper worked yesterday and returns nothing today. What is the likely cause?
options: The site changed its markup so your selector no longer matches - print what you actually received
Python needs to be reinstalled
The Beautiful Soup library has expired
The CSV file has run out of space

lessons.title: Build 3 Python Automation Scripts
objectives: Build one automation end to end, on your own machine and your own files
Make a script that changes things safe to run twice
Hand it to somebody who is not you and watch them run it
lessons.notes:
THIS IS THE SAME VIDEO YOU WATCHED IN MODULE 6, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. There you watched it straight through for the pattern. Here you watch it in short sections and BUILD, typing every line yourself. Pause after each section and get that piece running before you move on.

TYPE IT, DO NOT PASTE IT. Pasting a working script teaches you nothing. Typing it makes you meet every error, and the errors are the lesson - a misspelled variable, a missing colon, the wrong indentation. You will remember what you fixed.

BUILD THE ONE YOU CHOSE in module 6 - the chore you described as read, decide, write. If you did not choose one, build the file-renaming project, which is the safest place to start.

WORK ON COPIES. This is the first rule of any script that changes files: run it on a COPY of the folder, never the original, until it has done the right thing three times in a row. A renaming rule with one mistake in it can destroy the only copy of somebody's files in under a second, and there is no undo.

MAKE IT SAFE TO RUN TWICE. Ask what happens if it runs again by accident - which it will. Does it rename already-renamed files into nonsense? Does it send the same message a second time? Add a check that skips anything already done. This single habit is the difference between a script that helps and a script that causes an incident.

PRINT WHAT IT IS ABOUT TO DO. Before each change, print the old value and the new value. On the first run, comment out the line that actually makes the change so the script only prints what it WOULD do. Read those lines carefully. Then turn the change back on. Of everything in this course, this is the habit most worth keeping.

HANDLE THE ODD ONE OUT. Real folders contain a file with no extension, a name with an odd character in it, a spreadsheet that is open in another program and cannot be touched. Wrap the work for each item in try and except, from module 4, record the item that failed with enough detail to find it again, and carry on to the next one. One bad file must not end the run.

HAND IT OVER. Write a short comment at the top of the file: what this does, what to put where, how to run it. Then give it to somebody else and watch them run it without helping them. Whatever they get stuck on is the part you had not actually finished.
lessons.practice: Build and finish one automation script on your own files. It must do four things: print what it will do before doing it, be safe to run a second time, survive one bad item without stopping, and carry a comment at the top explaining how to run it. Then have somebody else run it unaided and write down where they got stuck.

quiz.question: Before letting a script change real files, what should you do?
options: Run it on a copy, with the change commented out so it only prints what it would do
Run it on the originals and check the result afterwards
Ask a friend to read the code through
Nothing, as long as the code runs without errors

quiz.question: Why must a script that changes things be safe to run twice?
options: An accidental second run must not redo the work - renaming already-renamed files or sending the same message again
Python requires every script to be run twice
It makes the script run faster the second time
It is only needed if you plan to sell the script

lessons.title: Landing Freelance Jobs with Python
objectives: Turn one finished script into a proposal somebody can say yes to
Price a first job without either insulting yourself or losing it
Run that first job so it ends in payment and a reference
lessons.notes:
THE SAME VIDEO AS MODULE 6, SECOND HALF. In module 6 the question was whether this work is realistic and what it consists of. Here watch the part on profiles, proposals and pricing - and this time act on it, because you now have a finished script from module 7 to sell.

ONE RESULT MATTERS MORE THAN A PROFILE. The script you finished in module 7 is the thing. Write it up in four lines: the chore, the hours it used to cost, what your script does, the minutes it costs now. That paragraph does more work than any profile page.

HOW TO OPEN WITH A LOCAL CLIENT: do not lead with Python. Lead with their problem. Something like - I noticed you spend your evenings copying statement lines into a spreadsheet, and I can make that four minutes, may I show you. Nobody buys a programming language. They buy the evening back.

THE PROPOSAL IS THREE SHORT PARAGRAPHS: what you understood them to need, what you will deliver and by when, and what it costs. No jargon at all. If you cannot describe the deliverable in one sentence, you do not yet understand the job - go back and ask more questions.

PRICING A FIRST JOB. There are two ways to get this wrong. Free makes the work worthless to both of you and it will never get finished. A large number you cannot justify loses the job and the relationship. Price the first one SMALL AND FIXED - a figure you would not resent losing an evening over - and say plainly that it is a first-job price. Fixed, not hourly, because you cannot yet estimate your own hours and you should not make the client pay for that.

HALF UP FRONT. Half before you start, half on delivery, agreed in a written message. This is completely normal, it is not rude to ask, and it quietly filters out the client who was never going to pay you at all.

PUT THE SCOPE IN WRITING. Name what is included and what is not. The commonest way a first job goes wrong is never the code - it is the fourth extra thing added after the price was agreed, which turns a small job into a month.

FINISH PROPERLY. Deliver the script with a plain instruction sheet, sit with them while they run it once themselves, then ask for two things: a few written sentences about the result, and permission to describe the work to others. Those two are worth more than the fee was.

DELIVERY BEATS BRILLIANCE. A modest script that is finished, documented and handed over beats a clever half-built one every single time.
lessons.practice: Write a one-page proposal for one of the real people you identified in module 6: their problem in their own words, the deliverable in one sentence, a delivery date, a fixed price, and an explicit list of what is not included. Then write the opening message you would send them. Do not send it until your module 7 script is actually finished.

quiz.question: How should a first job be priced?
options: Small and fixed, stated plainly as a first-job price, with half paid up front
Free, in order to build a reputation
Hourly, at the highest rate you can justify
Whatever the client offers to pay

quiz.question: What is the commonest way a first freelance job goes wrong?
options: Scope that was never written down, so extra work keeps being added after the price is agreed
A bug in the code
The client not knowing any Python
The script running too slowly

lessons.title: 5 Python Portfolio Projects That Get You Hired
objectives: Choose portfolio projects that prove something an employer cares about
Publish them so a stranger understands them in ninety seconds
Avoid the mistakes that make a portfolio count against you
lessons.notes:
WHAT A PORTFOLIO IS FOR. It answers one question a stranger is asking: can this person finish something. THREE FINISHED SMALL PROJECTS BEAT ONE AMBITIOUS UNFINISHED ONE, every time and without exception.

THE TUTORIAL TRAP. A portfolio made of the five most-followed tutorial projects on the internet proves only that you can follow instructions, and every reviewer recognises them on sight. Take a tutorial project and CHANGE it - different data, an extra feature, your own source. The change is your portfolio; the tutorial was only scaffolding.

CHOOSE PROJECTS THAT LOOK LIKE LOCAL WORK. A scraper that builds a list from a public Kenyan directory. A script that turns exported M-Pesa statements into a monthly summary. A tool that renames and files scanned documents for a small office. A small summary of publicly published county data. These read as somebody who solves problems here, which is a different impression from somebody who copied an American tutorial.

THE README IS THE PROJECT. Most employers will never run your code - they read the first screen of the repository and decide. It needs four things: one sentence on what this does, a screenshot or a sample of the output, how to run it, and one honest line on what it does not do yet. A repository with no README is invisible, however good the code inside it is.

PUT IT ON GITHUB and let the commits tell a story - several commits made as you built it, not a single commit called final. NEVER COMMIT KEYS OR PASSWORDS. Automated scanners find keys in public repositories within minutes of the push, and a leaked key in your portfolio is the fastest way to turn an interview into a polite no.

USE REAL DATA, NOT INVENTED DATA. A project that ran against genuinely messy real input, and says in the README what broke and how it was handled, is far more convincing than one that only ever ran against a tidy file you made up.

BE ABLE TO EXPLAIN EVERY LINE. The single most common way an interview ends badly is a candidate who cannot explain their own code. If a piece of it came from somewhere else and you do not understand it, either learn it properly or take it out.
lessons.practice: Take one project you have already built in this course and finish it as a portfolio piece: put it on GitHub with a README giving what it does, sample output, how to run it, and its current limits. Check the repository contains no keys or passwords. Then have somebody who does not code read the README and tell you what they think the project does - if they cannot, rewrite the first sentence.

quiz.question: Why is a portfolio of five well-known tutorial projects weak?
options: It proves only that you can follow instructions - changing a project with your own data or feature is what counts
Tutorials usually teach inaccurate code
Employers dislike video courses
Five projects is too many to review

quiz.question: What must never appear in a public repository?
options: Keys or passwords - automated scanners find them within minutes
A README file
Screenshots of the output
More than one commit
